title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 387
paragraphs: Apries having thus been overthrown, Amasis became king. He was from the district of Saïs, and the name of the city he came from is Siuph. At first the Egyptians despised Amasis and held him in little regard, because he had been a commoner of no distinguished family; but afterwards Amasis won them over by cleverness rather than obstinacy. Among countless other valuable possessions of his, there was a golden foot-basin in which both Amasis himself and all his guests always used to wash their feet. He broke this up, and from the metal he had an image of a god made, and set it up in the city, where it was most prominent. The Egyptians continually visited the image and paid it great reverence. Then Amasis, hearing what the townspeople were doing, called the Egyptians together and explained the matter to them, saying that the image had been made from the foot-basin into which the Egyptians had formerly vomited, urinated, and washed their feet, whereas now they were showing it great reverence. “And just so,” he continued, “I myself have now fared like the foot-basin; for though formerly I was a commoner, I am now your king,” and he bade them accordingly honor him and hold him in regard.
